articles.title: Letitia James stumped by debate question while GOP rival delivers 'zinger for the ages'
articles.summary: Letitia James went silent for several seconds when asked to name a former AG she admired during the Thursday New York Attorney General debate.
articles.body:
New York Democratic Attorney General Letitia James went silent for several seconds when asked to name a former state attorney general she admired during Thursday's New York attorney general race debate.

"Tick tock," Errol Louis of Spectrum News 1, one of the moderators said to James, prompting laughter from the Attorney General.

The attorney general's race in New York comes against the backdrop of James' ongoing dispute with President Donald Trump, who called James "a Complete and Total Disaster" and accused her of leading a "WITCH Hunt" against him in his endorsement of James' Republican challenger, Saritha Komatireddy, in August.

The pause from James drew immediate criticism from Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor and chief of staff for the Drug Enforcement Administration, who quipped from the podium that James "only admires herself."

"An absolutely devastating moment for Tish James," conservative communications strategist Steve Guest wrote on X . "'She only admires herself' is a debate zinger for the ages."

"No, no, no, no, we admire others," James said. "I admire all of the past attorney generals because it is a difficult job and you've got to stand up."

When asked the same question, Komatireddy named Dennis Vacco, who served as the state's attorney general from 1995 to 1998. Like Komatireddy, he was also a former federal prosecutor.

James then said that she admired former Democratic Attorney General Bob Abrams, who served from 1979 to 1993.

The exchange, which came in the final moments of Thursday's debate, led critics to question whether James knew of other New York attorneys general.

"Very telling moment," Steve McLaughlin, Rensselaer County executive, wrote on X. "James went completely blank because she's A: dumb as a rock B: has no idea who any former AG is because she's not doing the job and never has been."

"She's a mouthpiece," McLaughlin continued. "Zero institutional knowledge."

"Letitia James doesn't know the plural form of 'Attorney General,'" another Twitter user wrote.

Nicole Kiprilov, a spokesperson for Komatireddy, echoed the candidate's comment on the debate stage.

"Letitia James can't name a single former Attorney General she admires because she's too busy admiring herself. She's turned the Attorney General's office into her own political stage and ignored the safety of the state," Kiprilov said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "New Yorkers deserve a real prosecutor, not a joke like her!"

But James' campaign pushed back on Komatireddy's characterization of James and how she runs her office.

"Attorney General Letitia James spent much of the debate teaching her opponent how the Office of the Attorney General actually works, and she was happy to name former Attorney General Bob Abrams as someone she respects," a spokesperson for James said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

James' attorney general's office has been thrust into the national spotlight after New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special investigator to examine an alleged gang rape that occurred at Cornell University in October 2024. The renewed attention comes in response to a recent lawsuit filed by the alleged victim, Jane Doe, against the university, the alleged perpetrators, her sorority and a bar that allegedly served her alcohol while she was underage.

But James has faced calls from an attorney for one of the defendants to recuse herself from the case over social media posts showing support for Jane Doe before James was appointed special investigator.

articles.title: Who is Katie Zacharia, Trump's new White House press secretary?
articles.summary: The president described her as “a devoted fan and member of MAGA.”
articles.body:
President Trump announced on Friday that he has chosen Katie Zacharia, a conservative commentator, lawyer and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, as his new press secretary. Zacharia replaces Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August.

Zacharia "has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," the president wrote on social media . "She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!"

Zacharia called the appointment "the honor of a lifetime" in a post on social media.

To join the White House, Zacharia, 42, will exit her current role as senior communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social. Before that, she served for about two months as a deputy assistant secretary and spokesperson for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to her LinkedIn . Zacharia has also worked with Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State.

Zacharia is best known for her frequent appearances defending the administration's policies on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets. She told CNN in April — around the time she left DHS — that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol."

In his announcement, Trump said that Zacharia was "involved in my Campaigns, assisting in key Swing States." She wrote in a February New York Post column that she did "hard work helping flip Michigan red in Dearborn" in 2024.

Zacharia is a California native and self-described " lifelong conservative " who holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University in Malibu. She first came to Washington in 2006 to intern for the Republican National Committee while George W. Bush was president. She lives in California.

Citing a source familiar with internal White House discussions, CNN reported on Friday that "Zacharia's selection came about quickly" and that "she was not being considered for the role" as of "last week." CNN also reported that "on multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list" of possible press secretaries "only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position."

In her February New York Post column, Zacharia recounted a clash with liberal patrons of her "local cardio kickboxing gym" that ended with the gym owner asking her not to wear her red "Team Trump 2024" hat to exercise class.

"I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," Zacharia wrote. "I refuse to stay silent. My constitutional rights aren't negotiable. Tyranny thrives when good people lack courage."

articles.title: Bisnagas: Vigilância Sanitária adia prazo de mudança aos comércios | G1
articles.standfirst: Comerciantes de Presidente Prudente (SP) e de outras cidades terão prazo maior para adaptar as mudanças previstas pelo órgão fiscalizador, com data prevista para 1º de fevereiro de 2027.
articles.summary: Os comerciantes em Presidente Prudente (SP) já estavam sendo orientados pela prefeitura sobre a nova norma da Vigilância Sanitária estadual quando a data foi alterada.
articles.body:
Os comerciantes do setor de alimentos em Presidente Prudente (SP) já estavam sendo orientados pela prefeitura sobre a nova norma da Vigilância Sanitária estadual quando a data para o cumprimento das exigências foi adiada.

O Regulamento Técnico sobre Boas Práticas para Estabelecimentos Comerciais e Serviços de Alimentação devia entrar em vigor em 4 de outubro deste ano, mas a nova data foi fixada para 1º de fevereiro de 2027.

Entre as mudanças previstas no regulamento está a proibição de bisnagas coletivas de molhos. De acordo com o texto da portaria, o prazo foi adiado devido à complexidade das novas regras, que também mudam rotinas de preparo e boas práticas no setor.

O objetivo do fim das bisnagas é reduzir o risco de contaminação cruzada durante o consumo dos alimentos . No caso, evitar que o recipiente coletivo ajude a transferir microrganismos entre os clientes.

Comerciantes compartilham popularidade de molho verde em Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: David Jean/Arquivo pessoal

No caso de Presidente Prudente, a cidade carrega a fama pelo molho verde, oferecido na maioria das lanchonetes e comércios da região.

Diante disso, a Vigilância Sanitária municipal realizou quatro encontros, entre 17 e 28 de setembro, com representantes de supermercados e minimercados, restaurantes orientais, restaurantes comerciais (por quilo e self-service) e lanchonetes.

Mesmo com a prorrogação do prazo, o órgão orienta que os estabelecimentos já comecem as adequações.

“A Vigilância Sanitária orienta todos os estabelecimentos a já começarem, não esperar para a última hora para fazer as adequações. Ou seja, para ir retirando [as bisnagas] e acostumando o público dele a não utilizar mais a bisnaga”, orientou Paulo Gonçalves Rosa Neto, supervisor da Vigilância Sanitária de Presidente Prudente.

De acordo com o supervisor, a fiscalização continuará sendo realizada normalmente pelos fiscais do município.

“Nós vamos fazer orientação quanto às adequações. Não vai ter nenhum tipo de autuação ou coisa parecida, vai ser uma inspeção normal, rotineira, como de costume”, explicou o supervisor.

Entre as principais alterações apresentadas pela prefeitura durante os encontros estão:

Reforço com exigência de uniformes, proteção dos cabelos e restrições ao uso de barba, cílios e unhas postiças;

Controle mais rigoroso de temperatura e monitoramento no recebimento, armazenamento e exposição dos alimentos;

Novas regras para alimentos a granel, incluindo a proibição da comercialização de suplementos alimentares nessa modalidade;

Exigências específicas para culinária japonesa, como controle de pH do arroz e alerta ao consumidor sobre riscos de consumo de alimentos crus ou mal cozidos;

Regulamentação do delivery, com obrigatoriedade de lacre ou selo que indique violação e identificação de produto pronto para consumo imediato.

Pizza de frango com molho verde entra no cardápio de pizzaria de Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Pizzaria Vó Maria/Reprodução

Conforme a prefeitura, um dos pontos que mais impactam o dia a dia dos comércios é justamente a proibição do uso de bisnagas de uso coletivo para molhos e condimentos, comuns em mesas e balcões.

A partir da nova legislação, esses itens devem ser substituídos por embalagens individuais e descartáveis, como sachês ou porções unitárias.

Confira abaixo os artigos previstos na portaria da Vigilância Sanitária estadual, considerando a seção II - Armazenamento de produtos:

Art. 37. Parágrafo único - É vedado (proibido) reaproveitar embalagens em geral , bem como a utilização de sacolas de compras e sacos coletores de resíduos para armazenamento de alimentos.

Art. 39. Os alimentos pré-preparados e preparados devem ser armazenados de forma protegida e identificados com, no mínimo, as seguintes informações: designação do alimento, data de preparo e prazo de validade.

Art. 52. É vedado manter ou utilizar alimentos, matérias-primas e ingredientes com prazo de validade vencido, rasurado ou inexistente , com embalagens não íntegras, violadas, amassadas, enferrujadas, estufadas ou sem identificação de procedência. Também é vedado utilizar produtos mantidos fora das temperaturas recomendadas pelo fabricante ou estabelecidas neste regulamento.

articles.title: Alerta de chuvas: Defesa Civil avisa Bauru, Prudente e Itapetininga | G1
articles.standfirst: Alertas por SMS e Cell Broadcast são enviados conforme áreas de instabilidade avançam pelo estado de São Paulo. Neste sábado (10), os avisos foram encaminhados a nove municípios do interior.
articles.summary: Alertas por SMS e Cell Broadcast são enviados conforme áreas de instabilidade avançam pelo estado de São Paulo. Neste sábado (10), os avisos foram encaminhados a nove municípios.
articles.body:
Defesa Civil emite alerta de chuvas para cidades das regiões de Bauru, Prudente e Itapetininga — Foto: Beatriz Jarins/g1

A Defesa Civil do Estado de São Paulo emitiu alertas de chuva para cidades do interior paulista até as 17h30 deste sábado (10).

Ao todo, foram enviados 24 avisos, sendo 23 por SMS e um pelo sistema Cell Broadcast. Os alertas abrangeram municípios das regiões de Bauru, Itapetininga e Presidente Prudente.

Entre as cidades que receberam os avisos estão Assis, Maracaí, Caiabu, Dracena, Presidente Epitácio, Rancharia, Fartura, Itaporanga e Itararé.

Alerta cell broadcast foi enviado para Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Stephanie Fonseca/g1

Segundo o órgão, durante temporais, a população deve procurar um local seguro, como edificações fechadas distantes de áreas abertas em ocorrência de raios, afastar-se de árvores e evitar áreas alagadas.

Além disso, o cuidado com ventos fortes e a redução da velocidade enquanto dirige também são necessários em casos de tempestades.

O temporal que atingiu Cesário Lange (SP) na tarde de sexta-feira (9) provocou a queda de 62 árvores e causou estragos em diferentes pontos da cidade. Em oito horas, o município registrou 110 milímetros de chuva.

Defesa Civil de Cesário Lange informou que três carros foram atingidos pelas quedas de árvores — Foto: Defesa Civil de Cesário Lange/Reprodução

De acordo com a Defesa Civil municipal, a chuva começou por volta das 16h de sexta-feira. Até a manhã de sábado (10), foram contabilizadas a queda de 62 árvores na cidade.

As equipes atuam na remoção de árvores e na liberação de rodovias, estradas rurais e vias urbanas.

Para receber alertas da Defesa Civil por SMS, envie o CEP da sua localidade para o número 40199. Em caso de emergência, acione o Corpo de Bombeiros pelo 193 ou a Defesa Civil pelo 199.

articles.title: Sidônio Palmeira deixa Secom para reforçar campanha de Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Faltando 15 dias para a eleição, ministro entrará de vez para a equipe da campanha petista; políticos nordestinos assumiram a coordenação para o segundo turno
articles.summary: Sidônio Palmeira tira férias da Secom para integrar a coordenação da campanha de Lula no segundo turno, após mudanças na estratégia de comunicação petista.
articles.body:
O publicitário Sidônio Palmeira, ministro da Secretaria de Comunicação Social (Secom), durante cerimônia de assinatura do termo de posse, no Palácio do Planalto, em Brasília, nesta terça-feira, 14. — Foto: MATEUS MELLO/ENQUADRAR/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

O ministro da Secretaria de Comunicação Social da Presidência (Secom), Sidônio Palmeira, deverá tirar férias a partir de segunda-feira (12) para dedicar-se à campanha do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) à reeleição. A ideia é que o ministro reforce a equipe de comunicação do petista.

Faltando 15 dias para o segundo turno, a decisão vem logo depois de Lula trocar o comando de sua campanha. Políticos do Nordeste assumiram a empreitada . A parte de comunicação ficou sob o comando de Rafael Fonteles (PT-PI), governador reeleito do Piauí.

Sidônio tem sido alvo de críticas por focar a campanha na defesa da soberania e das terras raras, em vez de temas que impactam a rotina do eleitor. O próprio presidente Lula chegou a dizer que essa foi a campanha mais desorganizada que ele já fez .

Agora, o ministro foi pressionado a tirar férias para se dedicar inteiramente à campanha e se afastar da Secom nesse período.

Em 2022, Sidônio foi o marqueteiro que levou Lula ao terceiro mandato como presidente da República.

Apesar de até o momento não estar formalmente na campanha, Sidônio integra uma espécie de núcleo dirigente que auxilia Lula a definir as principais estratégias na disputa eleitoral, ao lado de Edinho, do ministro da Secretaria-Geral da Presidência, Guilherme Boulos (PSOL), e do presidente do Instituto Lula, Paulo Okamotto. Sidônio também é sócio de Raul Rabello, marqueteiro da campanha.

A troca da coordenação por petistas do Nordeste está relacionada a uma estratégia da campanha de ampliar a votação na região. Há um diagnóstico entre os petistas de que o Nordeste é a região com maior capacidade de Lula obter votos e reverter a vantagem de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

O afastamento, mesmo que temporário, de ministros e outros auxiliares do governo para participar da campanha tem sido realizado desde antes do primeiro turno.

O fotógrafo Ricardo Stuckert, auxiliar de confiança de Lula, pediu demissão do governo ainda em julho para se dedicar inteiramente à campanha. Stuckert ocupou o cargo de secretário de Produção e Divulgação de Conteúdo Audiovisual da Presidência e acompanha Lula há 23 anos com registros oficiais de eventos do presidente.

Logo antes do primeiro turno, ministros do governo e aliados se afastaram para se dedicar à campanha . Entre eles, Boulos e José Guimarães, ministro da Secretaria de Relações Institucionais da Presidência, que pediram licença temporária não remunerada.

Outro que se afastou temporariamente de suas funções logo antes da votação do primeiro turno foi o presidente do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), Aloizio Mercadante.

Aliado histórico de Lula, Mercadante foi responsável por elaborar o plano de governo de Lula na campanha do petista de 2022 ao Planalto.

articles.title: Pentagon's plan to livestream execution sparks backlash
articles.summary: "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," said GOP Sen. Thom Tillis.
articles.body:
Washington — The revelation that the Pentagon plans to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, has sparked intense pushback, with one Republican senator calling it "disgusting" and critics warning it could inspire more acts of terrorism.

On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed CBS News' reporting that the Dec. 3 execution will be livestreamed. Hegseth told Real America's Voice the execution would be public "because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth recommended, and President Trump approved, a plan to use an Army firing squad.

"Death penalty through firing squad, and he deserves it," Mr. Trump said during an unrelated White House event on Friday.

In an interview Friday night in Syracuse, New York, with WSTM-TV, President Trump said he "wasn't involved in that decision" to livestream the execution, "but I understand that decision."

"I guess they want to have it serve as an example, and I understand that very well," the president added.

Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is retiring, called the decision "beyond disgusting." Tillis voted to confirm Hegseth, but is now expressing his regret in doing so.

"Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting," Tillis wrote on X . "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America."

Republican Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia wrote on X , "I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that."

Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah urged Hegseth to reconsider.

"Seneca warned that Rome's bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them," he said on X . "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. Secretary Hegseth's plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider."

Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy said publicly executing someone is "medieval."

"That's disgusting. What, is he mimicking ISIS executions?" Murphy said on CNN . "I mean, I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions is medieval. It's frankly one of the things that we abhor about terrorist groups. And the fact that the United States is doing it — I just learned this, that is just absolutely extraordinary, galling. No matter whether you support or oppose the death penalty, public hangings and executions? That's what America has become?"

Ned Price, who was the State Department's spokesman during the Biden administration, said a public and livestreamed execution will create more "radicalized zealots."

"You can take it from those of us who've spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause," Price wrote on X . "Or take it from AQ and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth's proposal. Either way, it's hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America's image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable."

Alonzo Lunsford, a former U.S. Army sergeant who was shot seven times during the Fort Hood shooting but survived, said he supports the gunman's execution by firing squad. But Lunsford said this execution is "not something you should view for entertainment purposes."

"To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief," he told BBC Radio .

Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, issued a statement Friday morning urging the Pentagon to reconsider.

"In no way can [Hasan's] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered. The word of God exhorts us: 'do not repay anyone evil for evil,'" the archbishop said, citing Romans 12:17. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

Conservative talk show host Erick Erickson, who supports the death penalty, also said a public, livestreamed execution of Hasan will give him the "platform for martyrdom he wants."

"Hasan is a paraplegic, confined to a wheelchair," Erickson wrote . "The public imagery of a firing squad killing a man sitting in a chair because he cannot stand is going to undermine support for the death penalty. A society that increasingly finds ways to sympathize with the villains will do so here. This also gives Nidal Hasan the platform for martyrdom he wants. They'll be passing out the livestream video in the Middle East to inspire more terrorists to shoot up Americans to celebrate the glory of the martyrdom of Nidal Hasan."

Geoffrey Corn, a Texas Tech University law professor who served in the Army's Judge Advocate General's Corps, told CBS News that the plan to livestream the execution "raises significant moral questions, above and beyond the questions related to the death penalty generally."

"There's a certain protocol that is normally followed with executions limiting the gallery of observers, which usually includes people close to the victims and certain members of the media," he said.

Corn said "turning the execution of such a penalty into some type of public spectacle echoes of the past we seem to have put behind us."

Despite Lunsford's concerns about the livestream, the former U.S. Army sergeant said he'll be there for the execution.

"I'm going to be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude, you failed, I'm still here,'" he told the BBC.

The last public execution in the U.S. appeared to take place 90 years ago in 1936. That's when Rainey Bethea was hanged for rape in Kentucky. The execution reportedly drew a crowd of about 20,000.

Hegseth's announcement comes amid efforts from Democrats and Republican Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach him. A vote on his impeachment was delayed by House Speaker Mike Johnson's decision to cancel votes a day early ahead of the midterms.

articles.title: A small-town Alaska fisherman has Republicans on the defensive as they try to keep US House majority
articles.summary: JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — In the thick of Alaska's primary election season this summer, independent Bill Hill took a break from his U. House campaign to return h...
articles.body:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — In the thick of Alaska's primary election season this summer, independent Bill Hill took a break from his U.S. House campaign to return home to Bristol Bay.

The world's biggest sockeye salmon run was beginning, and that meant he needed to get back to work.

"I told my team that I have got to fish," he said, adding: "Commercial fishing is the way that we pay the bills."

Hill, 57, grew up in a tiny southwest Alaska village where he said his family had no phone and had to haul water from a nearby lake for cooking and bathing. Today, while he no longer has to fetch water, his lifestyle is not much different. He lives in a remote fishing community of about 430 people that he has called home for nearly half his life.

A retired teacher and school administrator, Hill has positioned himself as a working-class candidate who can relate to Alaskans' frustrations with high fuel and other costs. He has made affordability and pushing back against billionaires a central theme in his campaign against Republican Nick Begich, who's seeking a second term in Congress.

"We are pedal to the metal, making sure that every Alaskan knows about this campaign, every Alaskan knows what we stand for and every Alaskan knows that it's really one of them going to Congress," Hill told people at a campaign event this week in Juneau, wearing his standard campaign uniform of jeans, a zip-up vest and cap with a fishing company logo. "I need your help getting there."

The race has become a concern for Republicans as they are trying to hold onto their majority in the U.S. House. Vice President JD Vance held a rally this week for Begich and Dan Sullivan, the U.S. senator who also is in a tight reelection race. President Donald Trump is scheduled to do another in the coming week.

Begich and Republican political action committees have ratcheted up ad spending in the House race since the primary.

Planes, ferries and four-wheelers on the campaign trail

Hill, a first-time candidate who is Alaska Native, faces an incumbent from a prominent family long associated with the state's politics. Begich's late grandfather once held the state's only U.S. House seat. Begich's uncle Mark was a U.S. senator. Both were Democrats. Nick Begich is a lifelong Republican and has aligned himself with Trump, who has carried Alaska in his White House runs.

Hill's campaign said he has traveled more than 20,000 miles in the state, including by plane, ferry and all-terrain vehicle, to introduce himself to voters and promote his message.

Begich's name recognition presents a hurdle for Hill's campaign, but some Democrats tried to clear a better path for Hill. One suspended his campaign before the August open primary and endorsed Hill. Two other Democrats with virtually no name recognition withdrew after the primary despite being in line to advance.

One candidate registered as a Democrat remains in the top four, Eric Hafner. He has no apparent ties to the state and is incarcerated in New York.

Hafner received 3.8% of the vote, enough to qualify for the ranked vote general election on Nov. 3. His submitted candidate biography appearing in state election materials makes no reference to his stint in federal prison, where he is serving time for making threats against police officers, judges and others.

Hill's campaign has shared stickers showing Hafner in an orange jumpsuit and calling him a "fake 'Democrat.'"

"We want to make sure that the Alaskan people are well-informed," Hill said.

Begich gets support from Trump and the US House speaker

The contest has received national attention, with spending by groups that include the National Republican Congressional Committee and House Majority PAC, which seeks to flip the U.S. House to Democrats.

In early August, U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., held a rally for Begich that was closed to reporters. Vance called Begich a "machine" and effective legislator during his rally in Fairbanks, where Vance also gave support to Sullivan , who faces a challenge from Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman.

Trump has cited Begich's support of his signature package of tax breaks, social service cuts and immigration enforcement that was passed last year. The president plans to headline a rally Tuesday in Wasilla, hometown of Sarah Palin, the party's 2008 vice presidential nominee.

Hill said the visits show Republicans are nervous.

"I was not going to get into this race to waste people's time, to waste people's money," he said. "I did my due diligence before jumping in to ensure that there was a path to victory."

Begich's campaign did not respond to messages from The Associated Press. On social media, the campaign has highlighted events such as Begich's visit to the Alaska State Fair and recently has taken swipes at Hill.

Zach Bannon, an NRCC spokesperson, said Begich has delivered "commonsense wins for Alaska," including support of expanded oil and gas development. He called Hill a "far-left Democrat."

Hill was endorsed by Democrats but asserts his independence

Hill, who was endorsed by the Alaska Democratic Party, said he is a lifelong independent. He said he will not be beholden to a "party boss" or party line, and he rankled some voters earlier in the campaign by not explicitly saying which party he would caucus with in the House if he were elected.

He has said he is willing to work with anyone on what is best for Alaska. He also has called for bans on congressional stock trading and for limiting the influence of money in elections.

Hill said he wants to help build coalitions, saying he "can be a big part of a small group that makes big changes."

Democrat Bill Brown came to the Juneau event planning to vote for Hill but wanting to talk with him directly. He said they aligned on numerous issues, including support for the environment, schools and ending "forever" wars.

The retired economics professor said policy is important, but in this political moment he finds himself "most interested in the integrity of the candidate. Bill Hill convinced me on that issue."

Hill, who is Dena'ina Athabascan, said the top concerns he hears about from Alaskans are the price of fuel and overall cost of living. He said he had to fly home earlier this year and pump fuel oil from the textile manufacturing business he runs with his wife and bring it back to his house in a barrel because the community had run out.

He said fuel prices jumped from about $6.70 per gallon to about $9 per gallon after a barge shipment to his town earlier this year. Prices also have been higher elsewhere, particularly in communities accessible only by air or water. On social media, Hill's campaign calls out Begich for his support of the Iran war as it posts photos of fuel prices around the state.

Steve Davis, a voter at Hill's Juneau event this week, called him authentic and a "really good dude." He said he was drawn to Hill in part because he wants to see Congress reclaim its oversight role. Hill drew applause during the gathering when he said Congress must reassert itself as a separate but equal branch of government.

"We don't need a unified executive, we don't need kings," Davis said. "We need a Congress that actually functions."

articles.title: ‘Get in line:’ Donors strike new tone about helping Paxton
articles.summary: The perilous state of the GOP has led donors to accept whatever means necessary to hold the Senate.
articles.body:
For months, Republican donors insisted they didn't want to bankroll Ken Paxton's Texas Senate race after President Donald Trump endorsed him over long-time incumbent John Cornyn.

But polls have deteriorated in the weeks ahead of the midterm election so much so that many of these same donors are dropping their objections. The only thing that matters now, they say, is keeping the Senate – by whatever means necessary.

The change underscores the perilous state of the GOP, which finds itself confronting a darkening map where " the fires are everywhere " and which possibly portends the loss of multiple Senate races in states Trump won by double digits two years ago.

"The Senate's the firewall of freedom. As donors sort of handicap what is the most important factor for protecting policy priorities, it's the Senate," said Jason Thielman, former executive director of the NRSC and partner at political consulting firm S2R. "So you lick your wounds if your guy doesn't win and get in line."

MAGA Inc. and its affiliates are expected to spend almost $45 million on boosting Paxton, the state's attorney general, via direct mail, TV and digital advertising in Texas through Oct. 12.

But, with polls consistently showing Paxton trailing Democrat James Talarico, the Senate Leadership Fund, which is the GOP's top Senate super PAC, poured another $60 million into Texas to bring its spending in the Lone Star state to $131 million.

"In this difficult environment, only money can save some Republicans. Whatever bullets they have left they should use. Otherwise they might get blamed for any razor-thin defeats where more resources could have been the difference," said former Florida Rep. Carlos Curbelo.

SLF officials insist the Texas blitz isn't draining resources from other battlegrounds, claiming the entire nine-figure spend was raised through a dedicated state effort

"We're grateful for our enthusiastic donors who've stepped up and funded Texas PAC, SLF's dedicated effort to defeat Far-Left lunatic James Talarico," said SLF executive director Alex Latcham said in a text. "Their generosity ensured that we did not have to divert any resources from other key races and has allowed SLF to run effective campaigns across the map to defend the Senate majority."

The broader map is too tough to second guess decisions, according to eight donors, fundraisers, strategists and operatives, some of whom were granted anonymity to speak candidly on the state of the race.

"We are where we are. Do whatever necessary to hold the Senate," said a GOP fundraiser.

A GOP donor said it's also essential at this point to spend in other ruby-red states like Alaska, Kansas, which, like Texas, Trump won by double digits.

"Saving the Senate majority is the top priority if Trump wants to be able to confirm any judges or cabinet officials over the next two years," the person said in an e-mail. "Focus on shoring up AK, KS, ME, OH, IA and SC and play some offense in Michigan and New Hampshire if for no other reason than to make Democrats spend in those states."

Republicans are in triage mode , shifting money away from races they consider tougher to win. SLF is pausing its future spending in North Carolina and instead began spending to defend South Carolina, another state Trump won by double digits, and stepped up its advertising in Kansas.

Six GOP-held Senate seats, including in Texas and Kansas, are considered a toss-up by the nonpartisan handicapper Cook Political Report. The worrisome map for Republicans means any issues they have with candidates has to be set aside – and money spent from whatever pot that has it ready to deploy.

"Personal grievances or preferences, that's what primaries are for and that time has passed. This is about, are there considerations for making sure we have 51 senators and that's the whole ball game," said Mark Bednar, GOP strategist and former communications director to former Republican House Speaker Kevin McCarthy. "If that means people have to hold their nose from a money perspective and reinforce states that wouldn't be their first choice, we're past that point."

Inside the White House, senior officials make no distinction between different GOP pools of money as they look to shore up candidates across the country. MAGA Inc. and SFL cash are "one big giant bucket of money," a senior White House official said.

"That would be my message to any of the detractors: You know it's a team sport, and everyone needs to swim in the same direction, and that means whether it's MAGA, SLF, or whichever outside group, it's about spending enough money to get our candidates across the finish line," the person said.

A former Trump campaign official said that while donors "may have their own relationships or preferences in terms of" where their money gets spent, outside groups are "working together to make their message and ad buys right."

GOP donors have resigned themselves to the all-hands-on-deck approach, despite Trump pledging to pour "probably $400, $500 million" into the midterms from his MAGA Inc. PAC in September .

"I think at this point they're like, let's see what it takes," said a former Trump fundraiser. "They really don't see Trump stepping up helping Ken Paxton that much, and so they can't let an opportunity just disappear."

Still, MAGA Inc. has disclosed, as of last month, only spending a fraction of its over $400 million in the war chest on the midterm election, raising questions over why the president wants to hold onto the money.

A GOP lobbyist who has given to multiple Republican Senate campaigns called money "indeed fungible."

"But the tests will be whether MAGA Inc. dollars (a) actually get spent and (b) go to efforts that actually help candidates on the ballot vs promoting the president himself," the person added.

Megan Messerly contributed to this report.

articles.title: Congress should seal eligible records that keep Americans out of work
articles.summary: The author urges Congress to pass the bipartisan Clean Slate Act and the Fresh Start Act to remove federal record barriers that hinder employment and economic stability for many Americans.
articles.body:
I know what a second chance can make possible.

As a teenager, I faced court-ordered consequences, including a fine and community service. My record was ultimately expunged, and I went on to attend college and work for Republican members of Congress. Accountability and an opportunity to move forward both shaped my path.

That experience informs a question Congress should be asking: When people have met the law’s requirements and are ready to contribute, why leave unnecessary barriers in their way?

Lawmakers who want more people working, more families supporting themselves and better returns on taxpayer investments should pass the bipartisan Clean Slate Act. The legislation would remove barriers created by eligible federal arrest and conviction records, giving more Americans a meaningful opportunity to earn a living.

The Clean Slate Initiative’s recent report, “ The Economic Losses from Arrest and Conviction Records ,” estimates that arrest and conviction records are associated with $440 billion in lost earnings nationwide each year. The research finds persistent employment and earnings disadvantages even among people who were never convicted and those who went more than a decade without further contact with the legal system.

Compared with statistically similar peers without them, people with arrest or non-conviction records faced estimated annual earnings losses of $4,400. For people with nonviolent felony convictions, the estimate reached $9,300. Those are substantial sums for a family trying to cover rent, save for emergencies or put a child through college. Lower earnings also mean less spending at local businesses.

The $440 billion estimate covers records nationwide, beyond the federal records addressed by the Clean Slate Act, and record sealing alone cannot recover all those earnings. But the findings make the cost of leaving employment barriers unaddressed harder to ignore, and Congress can begin addressing that issue by fixing the federal records system it directly controls.

Consider the worker who completes a training program, earns a credential and applies for a job, only to encounter an old record that blocks the opportunity. The worker has done what policymakers asked, and yet, the employer loses access to a potential hire and taxpayers may have helped finance training that never translates into employment. A workforce strategy should address that last obstacle as seriously as it addresses the skills gap.

Employers should have access to qualified applicants, and people who have met the law’s requirements should have a meaningful opportunity to compete for work.

Public safety is central to second chances. A steady job gives someone a lawful income and responsibilities worth protecting. Helping people build stable lives should be part of how we prevent future crime. Blanket exclusion can undermine that goal, particularly when an old record tells an employer little about a person’s conduct today.

Taxpayers have a stake in what happens after a sentence ends. We should expect people returning to their communities to obey the law, find work and take responsibility for their families. The government should make those expectations achievable by removing unnecessary obstacles to employment.

When an eligible record continues to block a qualified applicant, it can undercut the very self-sufficiency our policies should encourage. Congress should evaluate record relief with the same practical question it brings to other public safety measures: Does this help create the conditions for people to remain law-abiding? A fair opportunity to earn a living belongs in that calculation.

The bipartisan Clean Slate Act , introduced in the House by Reps. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.) and Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) and in the Senate by Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) and Rand Paul (R-Ky.), offers a practical federal response. It would automate the sealing of qualifying federal non-conviction records and specified drug conviction records, subject to the bill’s requirements. It would also create a petition process for other eligible federal records. For someone never convicted, clearing an eligible arrest record gives practical meaning to the presumption of innocence.

The bill sets eligibility limits and preserves access for designated law enforcement and security purposes. Automated sealing applies the standards Congress establishes once the requirements are met. That reduces the paperwork burden on eligible people and allows the government to deliver relief consistently. A person’s ability to navigate an application should not determine whether they receive relief the law already makes available.

The bipartisan Fresh Start Act would complement that effort by helping states implement their own qualifying automated record sealing and expungement laws through federal infrastructure grants. Its reporting requirements would help the public assess implementation. Together, these measures would address federal record barriers and support states working to deliver relief under their own laws.

My own experience taught me what an opportunity to move forward can make possible. Congress should pass The Clean Slate Act and the Fresh Start Act so more people get those opportunities: putting their skills to work, providing for their families, and building stable futures. Accountability should open a path back to contribution, and our laws should make that path possible.

Reginald Darby is federal affairs director at the Clean Slate Initiative and a former congressional staffer.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new president who will agree to end the war
articles.summary: US leader suggests Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war amid tensions with Kyiv over a diesel deal with Russia.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump says Ukraine should replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy with a new leader, lashing out at him for Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries that have contributed to high diesel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump said at the White House on Saturday, adding that “for some reason [Zelenskyy] never does.”

Trump said that under Zelenskyy, Ukraine has “lost 30 percent of your country and you’ve had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That’s a war that should have never have started. And I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”

Following the remarks, Ukraine’s foreign minister defended Zelenskyy. “He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide,” Andriy Sybiga said in a post on X. “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.”

Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices ahead of the US midterms, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure.

He has also sought to blame record-high US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.

Trump suggested on Saturday that if he had been US president in 2022 “that war would have never started”.

“There was no reason that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence,” he said.

The remarks came hours after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, according to Ukrainian officials.

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed at least 60 people over the past four days.

On Friday, Trump said he had struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine.

He said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional three million tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he added.

The move drew a furious reaction from Zelenskyy. After Russia’s strikes on Saturday, he wrote on X: “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia”.

Zelenskyy said the attacks show Moscow understands “any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities.”

The president said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defences, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.

He also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and that Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16s used to intercept Shahed drones.

Ukraine’s European allies have expressed dismay at the Russian deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.

Trump’s announcement about the deal was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel the war against Ukraine.

Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war.

articles.title: Supreme Court climate case could bankrupt oil companies, send gas prices soaring, experts warn
articles.summary: Energy experts warn the Supreme Court's Suncor v. Boulder case could trigger thousands of climate liability lawsuits that raise gas prices.
articles.body: A Supreme Court showdown over climate change lawsuits could leave oil companies bankrupt, gas stations facing financial ruin and Americans paying more at the pump if the justices allow cities and states to pursue billions in damages against the fossil fuel industry, energy policy experts warn. "You would see mass exodus and that would create more scarcity with fuel, more so than we're seeing already today, higher prices," Jason Isaac, CEO of American Energy Institute, told Fox News Digital. "And that's really what this is about. It's about controlling these companies and stopping the use of hydrocarbons." The Supreme Court heard arguments Monday in Suncor v. Boulder, a dispute over whether federal law prevents cities and states from suing oil companies under state law for alleged climate damage linked to emissions that cross state borders. During oral arguments, Justice Clarence Thomas pressed Boulder's attorney, Kevin Russell, on whether the legal theory could expose businesses beyond oil producers to similar lawsuits, including large retailers. WAVE OF OVERLOOKED 'LEFT-WING' LAWSUITS COULD COME WITH AN UNEXPECTED PRICE TAG FOR AMERICANS "Nothing in our theory prevents that," Russell acknowledged, although he noted that state tort law could impose additional limitations. Justice Brett Kavanaugh separately raised concerns about the potential financial consequences of widespread litigation, warning that enough lawsuits could "bankrupt" defendants and questioning whether virtually any manufacturer or business could face similar claims. The city and county of Boulder, Colo., sued oil giants ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy in 2018, accusing the companies of knowingly contributing to climate change while misleading the public about the alleged dangers of fossil fuels. The municipalities are seeking damages to help cover the mounting costs of climate-related harms. There are roughly 30 similar lawsuits pending in jurisdictions across the country, including cases in Portland and Baltimore. Boulder's lawsuit alleged ExxonMobil and Suncor knew for decades about the climate risks associated with fossil fuels but misled the public about those risks. The complaint pointed to a 1977 internal memo from ExxonMobil that circulated among the company's highest-level managers. The memo reported that "current scientific opinion overwhelmingly favors" that fossil fuels contribute to the rise in CO2 emissions. David Bookbinder, who previously served as counsel of record for Boulder but is no longer involved in the case, described the lawsuit as a way to implement an "indirect carbon tax" during a Federalist Society forum last year. But Boulder has maintained that the case is not an attempt to regulate national climate policy, arguing instead that Colorado has the authority to hold companies accountable under state law for alleged harms suffered within its borders. "Since the founding, states have had the power to provide tort remedies for injuries occurring within their borders even when the conduct causing those injuries occurred elsewhere," Russell told the justices. CATHOLIC SCHOOLS, BANNED RIFLES AND ‘CLIMATE LAWFARE’: BLOCKBUSTER FIGHTS AWAIT SUPREME COURT O.H. Skinner, executive director of the Alliance for Consumers, argued that the lawsuits are an attempt to accomplish through the courts what climate advocates have been unable to achieve through Congress. "When you really boil it down, and you separate it from all the legal arguments, the advocates who push these cases are very clear," Skinner told Fox News Digital. "That it's an effort to get a backdoor carbon tax, because carbon taxes have never passed in Congress, or to bankrupt the energy industry." Justice Samuel Alito has recused himself from the case without providing an explanation. Isaac warned that a Supreme Court ruling in Boulder's favor could open "Pandora's box," allowing thousands of jurisdictions to pursue similar lawsuits. He said a 4-4 split could have a similar practical effect by leaving the lower court's ruling in place, although a tie would not establish nationwide precedent. "There are over 90,000 levels of government — government entities just in the United States alone — that could also begin lawsuits against energy companies," Isaac told Fox News Digital. "Driving up cost to consumers because the cost to defend those would be astronomical." LAWSUITS COST EVERY AMERICAN HOUSEHOLD THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS. SUPREME COURT CAN HELP Skinner argued that who could be sued could extend beyond oil producers to businesses across the energy supply chain, including gas stations, automakers and utilities that sell or use fossil fuels. "From Boulder's perspective, anybody who's contributed to climate change would reliable, any sort of company, big or small, and the problem here is that to the left, climate change is everything and everything is climate change," Skinner told Fox News Digital. "So it's very hard to find a line for who isn't contributing to climate change." But Isaac said the case is different from lawsuits against tobacco or opioid companies because greenhouse gas emissions come from countless sources around the world and cross state and national borders, making it difficult to isolate responsibility for climate-related damage. "Emissions are a global phenomenon," Isaac told Fox News Digital. CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION ExxonMobil and Suncor argue that because greenhouse gas emissions travel globally, Colorado cannot use state law to hold companies liable for emissions originating outside its borders. The companies contend that such disputes should instead be governed by federal law. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Meanwhile, other states such as Utah have barred these types of state tort lawsuits from being pursued. "If the energy companies were to lose and Colorado were to win, this would in effect drive up the prices of gas all across the country," Utah Attorney General Derek Brown told Fox News Digital. "And so those kind of decisions ultimately, it's the province of Congress."

articles.title: Sunday shows preview: Trump admin’s Russia deal, public execution plan spark pre-midterm backlash
articles.summary: President Trump struck a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel Friday, allowing the Kremlin to supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace, sparking a feud between him and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The deal served to remedy rising energy prices fueled by the U.S.’s ongoing military operations in Iran…
articles.body:
President Trump struck a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel Friday, allowing the Kremlin to supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace, sparking a feud between him and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

The deal served to remedy rising energy prices fueled by the U.S.’s ongoing military operations in Iran and Russia’s war in Ukraine. But Zelensky saw the move as a way to help Russia earn more money to fund its military offensive against his country. Trump responded Saturday by decrying the Ukrainian president’s Russian oil refineries strikes and called for his replacement.

“He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump said of Zelensky before traveling to Tennessee Saturday.

The decision has already drawn criticism from Democratic lawmakers , including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who accused Trump of “making a deal with the devil” — echoing Zelensky’s warning the deal may signal to Russia “it could simply keep attacking” Ukraine.

Zelensky is set to appear on ABC News’s “This Week” Sunday.

In September, Trump had signed bills targeting Russia and Iran, which imposed tariffs of up to 100 percent on the top five purchasers of Russian energy or on countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions.

At the time, GOP lawmakers, such as Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and John Kennedy (R-La.), championed the legislation. Cruz and Kennedy, along with former Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway, are set to appear on Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures” — where they will likely weigh in on the divisive deal.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also announced this week that convicted mass shooter Nidal Hasan’s execution by firing squad would be livestreamed on Dec. 3 in Texas amid a growing conversation surrounding the death penalty — brought back into the public eye after the late September botched lethal injection attempts against death row inmate Christa Pike.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted of fatally shooting 13 people and injuring 32 others in a 2009 attack against a Fort Hood, Texas military base.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), along with a slew of Democratic lawmakers, were quick to criticize Hegseth’s decision, with the North Carolina senator calling the proposal “beyond disgusting.”

“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America,” Tillis wrote on social platform X .

Pope Leo XIV weighed in on the debate Saturday, calling capital punishment “inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person” in a social media statement.

Tillis will likely discuss his denouncement of Hegseth’s plan during his Sunday NBC’s “Meet The Press” appearance. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), who similarly criticized the Pentagon chief’s decision to livestream the execution, is appearing on CBS’s “Face The Nation.”

Along with facing these high-profile Trump administration controversies, some GOP lawmakers and candidates are beginning to split with the president’s aggressive immigration enforcement agenda with less than a month before November’s midterms. Multiple Republican senators told The Hill the feared these moves would impact the party’s electability.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), who’s running for reelection this year, advised the Trump administration to ease off on immigrants who “are here and that have a court determination that [says] they can be here.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) broke records for the second Trump administration, with back-to-back months of arrests topping 50,000 in July and August, according to the Deportation Data Project. The group added that 55 percent of those detained had no criminal record, while another 24 percent had faced charges but were never convicted.

Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin is appearing on CNN’s “State of the Union,” where he will likely discuss this escalation. He may also weigh in on the criticism agency received following a high-profile shooting in the Bronx this week, during which a 28-year-old man was shot in his car while his 5-year-old child was also inside.

Following the shooting, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani slammed ICE’s actions in a statement, saying that he called Mullin and Trump for two hours after the incident. The mayor was “unsuccessful” in securing Belgal’s release from federal custody, he said.

Mullin will be appearing on Fox’s “Fox News Sunday” and on CBS’s “Face The Nation .”

It is one month until the 2026 midterm elections with the GOP entering a rocky midterm environment as the president’s approval rating continually declines and dissatisfaction with the ongoing conflict with Iran grows in the U.S.

Trump is expected to travel to Alaska and other battleground states in an effort to boost the GOP’s chances this fall as the Senate is considered a toss-up by polling averages.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 76 percent chance of flipping the House and a 56 percent chance of taking back the Senate.

House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) has remained confident despite the polling. He told The Hill’s broadcasting partner NewsNation in September he believed Republicans could retain the House. While other GOP leaders, including Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) acknowledged the party needed to “do more” to lower costs for Americans to keep control.

Emmer is set to appear on ABC’s “This Week,” while Barrasso will appear on CBS’s “Face The Nation.”

Texas Democratic Chair Kendall Scudder is set to unpack Democrat’s odds for gaining control of the upper chamber on News Nations’s “The Hill Sunday.” Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed will also appear on NBC’s “Meet The Press,” while Democratic New Hampshire Senate candidate Rep. Chris Pappas (D) will be on CBS’s “Face The Nation.”

See the full list of guests on the Sunday morning news shows below:

NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday”: Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt (R), Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder, Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller

CBS News’s “Face the Nation”: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.); Palantir Technologies CTO Shyam Sankar

CNN’s “State of the Union”: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin; Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft

Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday”: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn (R)

NBC News’s “Meet the Press”: Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.); Michael Lewis, author and journalist

Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures”: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), former Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway

ABC News’s “This Week”: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), Senate candidate and pastor Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.)

articles.title: Midterms could decide Johnson’s fate as GOP fights to hold House
articles.summary: Questions surrounding Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) political future are in the spotlight after he floated the possibility of returning to Louisiana if Republicans lose the House in November. The GOP is facing harsh political headwinds ahead of Election Day, as Democrats seek to capitalize on voter frustration over the economy and President Trump’s low approval…
articles.body:
Questions surrounding Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) political future are in the spotlight after he floated the possibility of returning to Louisiana if Republicans lose the House in November.

The GOP is facing harsh political headwinds ahead of Election Day, as Democrats seek to capitalize on voter frustration over the economy and President Trump’s low approval ratings. Republicans are defending a narrow House majority, leaving little room for error as Democrats target competitive districts across the country.

Decision Desk HQ forecasts that Democrats are favored to win back the House next year. A Democratic takeover would cost Johnson his Speakership and force Republicans to reckon with questions about their leadership and the party’s direction.

One GOP lawmaker, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to The Hill, said some Republicans could seek a leader who is willing to serve as a check on the Trump administration if Democrats flip the House.

“I hear it all the time in the District. We want a check and balance. We don’t want a rubber stamp,” the lawmaker said, adding that they think this will “hurt” the party in the election.

Johnson, a staunch ally of the president, has worked to hold his slim majority together while contending with repeated division within his conference, including clashes over government funding and the Iran war.

“Heaven forbid, if we lose this majority or whatever, I don’t know what my next chapter of life is,” Johnson told Fox News in an interview this past week.

“If God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I’ll do that with equal fervor. I mean, I just want to be of my highest and best use to God and to my country.”

His remarks quickly reverberated through Washington, so much so that his spokesperson, Lance Trover, dismissed any speculation that Johnson would leave Capitol Hill.

“All the DC speculation about the Speaker because he dared to speculate about his potential future in the lawn care business is hilarious,” Trover wrote on the social platform X . “Not that I believe he’d be bad at it, but allowing it to overshadow the massive fundraising numbers announced this morning or the insane travel schedule he’s doing to keep the majority seems to be nothing short of trying to drive a contrived narrative.”

Still, some GOP lawmakers and aides told The Hill that there could be a potential push to support someone else as leader besides Johnson if the party suffers major losses in the midterms.

“I think Mike could have done a better job, but it wasn’t just him,” the same House member said. “It’s the whole leadership team.”

He added that he wasn’t “shocked” by Johnson’s remarks, noting that former GOP House Speaker Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) announced he was going to retire months before Democrats won control of the House in the 2018 midterm elections.

A GOP staffer, meanwhile, said that if Republicans lose next month by a large margin “there will be a clear retreat.”

“I would imagine there to be more of a push for someone else,” the staffer added, noting the millions of dollars spent by the GOP on the election so far.

GOP strategist Amy Koch told The Hill it can be hard for a Speaker to return to the rank and file. There also tend to be more opportunities in the private sector for members fresh out of the Speakership.

Yet, she noted, if Democrats flip the House, it’s possible Johnson keeps the gavel given his “unusual” ascension to lead the party.

“Speaker Johnson came in under, really, a compromise situation,” she said, adding that the conference could be “happy to have him stay” should the GOP lose its majority.

“Some of that will play into whether he decides to go or not,” Koch concluded.

There’s also the Trump factor. The president could weigh in and urge Republicans to rally behind Johnson as minority leader, particularly given their close working relationship and the Louisiana Republican’s pro-Trump track record in Congress.

Still, some GOP staffers floated House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) as contenders for minority leader if Republicans lose the House. In August, Scalise dodged a question from Punchbowl News about whether he would seek the post.

One aide noted that the Republican conference at large “likes” Johnson and speculated that his personal friendship with Jordan could factor in to the Ohio Republican’s political future.

“I don’t know if … they lost the House if … Jim Jordan would then step in, and Mike Johnson would step aside,” they continued.

A different GOP lawmaker described Johnson as an “extraordinary Speaker.”

“I don’t think anyone could have done a better job than he has done,” they added.

A staffer told The Hill that chatter about the Speaker’s political future “is pure noise,” while another aide said it’s “nice” Johnson has been “transparent” on his thinking.

Johnson, for his part, maintained that he would be the Speaker of the next Congress.

“I’m not going to talk about the scenario where we don’t win the House, because I am laser-focused on winning the House,” he told Fox News when asked whether he would run for minority leader.

articles.title: Yemeni government’s military says its forces advancing against Houthis
articles.summary: Saudi-backed forces say 1,150 Houthis killed in operations against the Iran-aligned group over the past 24 hours.
articles.body:
The military of Yemen’s internationally recognised government says it has killed hundreds of Houthi fighters in targeted operations over the past 24 hours.

Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemeni government forces, said at least 1,150 Houthis were killed in almost 2,000 targeted operations across the country as part of operation “Dawn of Yemen”.

He said the army had destroyed Houthi ammunition dumps and at least 180 combat, transport and supply vehicles operated by the Houthis, adding that ground forces “continued to advance their assault”.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the information.

An attack on King Khalid International airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, on Saturday killed and injured several people and led to flights being cancelled.

When asked if the United States would join strikes against the Houthis after the attack, President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he “will make a decision soon”.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Yemen on Saturday, said the Houthis had yet to claim responsibility for the latest attack.

But the Iran-backed group has warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating there – except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina – is a target.

Mawry said the Houthis were preparing to fight the war on multiple fronts, including against the participation of international actors, such as Pakistan.

“The Houthis say that if Pakistan engages in any military activities against them on behalf of Saudi Arabia, then they will be treated in the same fashion as the Saudis are currently being dealt with,” Mawry said.

There are plans to launch ballistic missiles towards Pakistan and attack Pakistan-flagged vessels in the Red and Arabian seas, he added.

“The fighting is spreading on multiple fronts, but it is a situation that will keep escalating,” Baraa Shiban, an associate fellow in international security and Yemen expert at the London-based Royal United Services Institute think tank, told Al Jazeera, adding that the violence will not be “dying down” anytime soon.

“There is no mediation happening this time – there [are] no regional or local mediators that are able to cool down the situation,” he said.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are advancing on the Houthis in a bid to recapture areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical trade route for global shipping into and out of the Red Sea.

Battles are now raging around the strategic southern Yemeni cities of Mocha and Dhubab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of Bab al-Mandeb.

The Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014, seized the area in September, effectively taking control of the strait, although both sides claim control of the shipping lanes.

articles.title: President talks 'Trump Ocean,' trades jokes with Tennessee crowd as Kid Rock kicks off sprawling rally
articles.summary: Trump called Iranian leaders "crazy" and floated renaming an ocean after himself during a wide-ranging Tennessee rally with Kid Rock opening.
articles.body: President Donald Trump touted billions of dollars in manufacturing investments and his administration's efforts to combat crime in Tennessee on Saturday, while calling Iranian leaders "crazy" and floating the idea of a "Trump Ocean" during a wide-ranging rally featuring musician Kid Rock. The president appeared in Clarksville ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, campaigning for Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty and gubernatorial candidate Marsha Blackburn while mixing economic talking points, foreign policy and off-script humor. Kid Rock opened the event with a religious-themed introduction, praising Trump's leadership while taking aim at the news media. TRUMP TOUTS ‘GOLDEN AGE’ AT OHIO RALLY, URGES VOTERS TO DELIVER GOP MIDTERM WINS "Literally, President Trump could walk across the Cumberland River, and tomorrow the headline would say President Trump refuses to swim," the musician joked. The rocker also condemned Islamist extremism and defended religious freedom, arguing that Americans should not be forced to live under religious laws that override the Constitution. "We are not, and we will never be, one nation under Mohammed, because we are, and we always will be, one nation under God," Kid Rock told the crowd. Trump later thanked his longtime supporter and friend by his given name, Bob, before turning to an array of domestic and international issues. The president addressed tensions with Iran, calling the country's leaders "crazy" while claiming that Tehran's rhetoric had softened following U.S. military operations. AFTER 'LAKE AMERICA,' TRUMP SUGGESTS A NEW NAME FOR THE STATE OF NEW MEXICO "They don't talk that way anymore, by the way," Trump said after recounting previous threats from Iranian leaders. Trump described what he characterized as extensive damage to Iran's military capabilities, claiming 159 ships had been sunk and its air force and air-defense systems destroyed. "They have no Navy. They have no Air force, they have no anti-aircraft equipment," Trump said. The president then pivoted from the Strait of Hormuz to an unexpected geography lesson, suggesting it could one day be called the "Trump Strait." He also revisited his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America before floating additional changes to the map. "We need a river. We need an ocean," Trump said, suggesting the Atlantic or Pacific could become the "Trump Ocean" or "Ocean of the Americas." TRUMP RALLIES NEW YORK CROWD FOR REPUBLICAN BRUCE BLAKEMAN'S BID TO REPLACE GOV KATHY HOCHUL "Before I get out, I think we should have an ocean," he added, without yet announcing any formal renaming plans. On the economy, Trump promoted Korea Zinc's planned investment of more than $6 billion in Tennessee, a project expected to create 740 jobs across Montgomery and Smith counties. Tennessee officials announced the $6.6 billion project in December, describing it as the largest single private corporate investment in state history. The plans include a new critical-minerals smelter in Clarksville and the reopening of a former mine in Gordonsville. "And your state will soon be home to the first new mineral smelter in the United States, first one built since 1979," Trump said. The project is intended to strengthen domestic supplies of minerals used in semiconductors, defense technology and advanced manufacturing. TRUMP NAMES LEAVITT SUCCESSOR AFTER WEEKS OF SPECULATION — AND SHE'S NO STRANGER TO MAGA Trump also cited General Motors' previously announced $275 million investment in its Spring Hill manufacturing facility to support production of next-generation turbocharged Cadillac engines. The president credited his tariff policies with encouraging domestic investment, arguing that companies were expanding American manufacturing to avoid import duties. In a Tennessee-focused fact sheet released as the rally began, the White House asserted that Republican-backed tax policies had preserved $23 billion in economic activity in the state. The administration also cited an average $3,674 tax refund for Tennesseans in 2026. Public safety was another focal point of his address, with Trump praising federal law-enforcement operations in Memphis and claiming approximately 12,000 dangerous criminals had been removed. The White House separately asserted that murders and overall crime in Memphis had declined approximately 36%, crediting the Memphis Safe Task Force. The president also shared some lighter moments about first lady Melania Trump, describing her objections to his theatrical impersonations of athletes during discussions about transgender participation in women's sports. "She said it's not presidential," Trump recalled, before joking about her film career. "There is only room for one star in a family, so I don't need this movie stuff. I don't need it." Trump, who carried Tennessee in all three of his presidential campaigns, said the visit was also an opportunity to thank supporters in a state where he had enjoyed strong electoral backing. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Sometimes it's nice to go to a place where you don't have to be, but you're there to say thank you to the great people that elected you three separate times in record time," Trump said. Trump repeatedly returned to the November elections, urging supporters to back Republican candidates even though his name will not appear on the ballot. "In this election, I'm asking you to do me a favor. Pretend. Just pretend that I'm running," Trump said.

articles.title: Trump says he will ‘ultimately make decision’ on Fort Hood shooter execution livestream
articles.summary: President Trump said he will “make a decision ultimately” on whether to livestream the execution by firing squad of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan following GOP backlash. “He’s a vicious killer, killed 13 people in cold blood, wounded over 20. Some of those people will never have their lives back in a true sense,”…
articles.body:
President Trump said he will “make a decision ultimately” on whether to livestream the execution by firing squad of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan following GOP backlash.

“He’s a vicious killer, killed 13 people in cold blood, wounded over 20. Some of those people will never have their lives back in a true sense,” Trump told reporters on the White House South Lawn on Saturday. “He was vicious. He was violent.”

“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it, because you know by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” the president continued. “So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

Trump’s remarks come after he said on Friday that “they’re making a determination about” the decision to livestream Hasan’s death “but he will be killed, it will be through firing squad.”

“So, I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him,” Trump stated.

A White House spokesperson confirmed earlier this week that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “recommended” Hasan’s execution be carried out by firing squad on Dec. 3, and President Trump “approved” it.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center in November 2009, killing 12 soldiers and one civilian. He injured 32 others in what was the deadliest mass shooting ever on a U.S. military installation.

During his 2013 trial, Hasan acted as his own attorney, saying in his opening statement, that the “evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter,” adding that he carried out the mass shooting in response to the U.S. wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Vice President J.D. Vance told reporters Friday that he will not be watching the execution should it be livestreamed, even stating, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”

If Hasan is executed in December, it will be the military’s first execution in six decades. The plan to livestream it drew fierce criticism from Republicans and Democrats .
