articles.title: GOP sees House prospects grow bleaker as districts shift to blue
articles.summary: Less than a month out from the midterm elections, the landscape for House Republicans grows grimmer by the day. President Trump’s approval ratings are low and sinking. The GOP’s emergency redistricting campaign has fallen short of its goals. And the volatile economy has voters on edge and thirsty for change. The combination has created a…
articles.body:
Less than a month out from the midterm elections, the landscape for House Republicans grows grimmer by the day.

President Trump’s approval ratings are low and sinking. The GOP’s emergency redistricting campaign has fallen short of its goals. And the volatile economy has voters on edge and thirsty for change.

The combination has created a minefield of trouble for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and other GOP leaders, who are scrambling against increasingly long odds to keep their slim hold on the lower chamber in the next Congress.

The strength of the headwinds they face has become evident in recent weeks as the nation’s top election analysts have shifted their projections for dozens of House seats — almost all of them in the Democrats’ favor.

Those changes signal that Republicans are struggling not only in purple battleground districts — the traditional combat zones where majorities are usually won and lost — but also in much redder regions of the country where Trump won easily just two years ago.

Part of that is expected. Midterm elections are historically tough for the party that controls the White House. But experts say the challenges for Republicans have been compounded this cycle by the high cost of consumer goods — which can be linked directly to Trump’s policies, including tariffs and the Iran War — and the erosion of support for the president, whose approval rating is at historic lows.

“Republicans holding on to the House would be a shock given where the overall numbers are,” Kyle Kondik, the managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an independent election handicapper based at the University of Virginia, said Friday in an email.

The latest wave of bad news for Republicans came on Friday, when forecasters at the Cook Political Report, another non-partisan election analyst group, moved 18 House races towards the Democrats. The highlights of that report include:

Two incumbent Republicans who were previously favored to win, Reps. Bill Huizenga (Mich.) and Rob Whitman (Va.), are now in “toss up” races, meaning they’re too close to call.

Five “toss up” races are now in the “leans Democrat” category, including four GOP incumbents — Iowa Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, and Pennsylvania Reps. Scott Perry and Ryan Mackenzie — who are now predicted to lose. (The fifth lawmaker in that group is Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a centrist Washington Democrat who has been a top target of Republicans in a district Trump carried by 3 points in 2024. Cook now has her favored to win).

Three of the more vulnerable Democratic incumbents — Reps. Tom Suozzi (N.Y.), Laura Gillen (N.Y.) and Susie Lee (Nev.) — are now “likely” to keep their seats.

And highlighting the limits of the Republicans’ redistricting campaign, the group also moved Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.), who was thought to be drawn out of contention by North Carolina Republicans, into the “toss up” category.

Erin Covey, the Cook analyst behind the report, said the environment is such that “the most likely outcome” is that Democrats — who need to flip just three seats to win the majority — will pick up between nine and 19.

“At this point, Democrats only need to win 20% of the Toss Ups to get to a majority, assuming the seats that favor Democrats in our ratings all break their way,” Covey wrote.

The analysts at Sabato have reported a similar trend, moving more than 20 seats towards Democrats since the middle of September. Kondik, the managing editor, said much of the Republicans’ troubles can be attributed to the high cost of living.

“High prices can destroy a political coalition — it happened to the Democrats and now it’s happening to the Republicans,” he said.

Republicans are pushing back against the analysts’ predictions. They’re pointing to three factors that leave them confident they can repel a blue wave and keep control of the House next year.

First, they note that Republicans, boosted by a late spending spree from MAGA Inc., Trump’s super-PAC, have a clear cash advantage heading into the final stretch of the campaign. Second, most of the seats Democrats are hoping to flip are not in purple, 50-50 districts, but more conservative regions where Trump won by large margins. And third, the approval rating of Democrats is also well underwater.

“Voters might not like Republicans, they might not like Trump, but they don’t like Democrats. And you have to present them with a viable alternative, especially when you’re playing in this deep-red territory where they are Republican voters,” a national GOP operative said Friday by phone.

“If we turn out our base, they might hold their nose and vote for our guy, but they sure as hell are not going to vote for a Democrat,” the operative continued. “And they’re going into these districts that Trump won by 15, 20 points — that’s a huge uphill climb.”

Still, there’s no question that voters are restless, and recent polls suggest they’re ready to take it out on the party that controls all the power. A new survey, released Friday by the Pew Research Center, found that 68 percent of respondents — and 31 percent of Trump’s 2024 voters — disapprove of his performance.

Even Johnson, who has maintained throughout the cycle that Republicans will hold the House next year, recently acknowledged the possibility that he might lose the gavel.

“Heaven forbid, if we lose this majority or whatever, I don’t know what my next chapter of life is,” Johnson told Fox News last week . He quipped that he might return to Shreveport “and start a lawn business.”

On the bright side for Republicans, they’re expected to benefit from the retirement of Rep. Jared Golden, a Maine Democrat who had built his own independent brand and survived a number of tough challenges in a district Trump won by more than 9 points in 2024. That seat is now predicted to swing to the GOP.

But that pick-up is also expected to be offset by another retirement, that of GOP Rep. Don Bacon in Nebraska, where the Democrat is now favored to win the open seat encompassing Omaha.

Much of the outcome in the House could hinge on the effects of state redistricting.

Pressed by Trump, a number of GOP-led states re-drew their House maps this cycle in ways specifically designed to help Republicans. That practice, highly unusual in the middle of the decade, was intended to insulate Republicans from losing their majority by turning a number of blue seats to red.

In part, that campaign is predicted to bear fruit, as the new maps are expected to flip Democratic seats currently held by Reps. Shomari Figures in Alabama, Steve Cohen in Tennessee and Cleo Fields in Louisiana.

But several Democratic states retaliated with new maps of their own. And the gains that Republicans had initially intended are, in many cases, now much less certain given the national mood and momentum shift towards Democrats.

In Texas, for instance, where Republicans sought to bump off five Democrats, they might now get only two, as Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez are favored to win, according to Sabato’s experts, while GOP Monica De La Cruz is facing an unexpectedly tough contest. Cook analysts rank it a “toss up.”

In Florida, Republicans targeted four Democratic seats. But three of those races — including those featuring Democratic Reps. Jared Moskowitz and Kathy Castor — are in the “toss up” category, making them no slam dunk.

A similar dynamic is happening after redistricting in Ohio, where Republicans had sought to flip two seats with their new maps. But Rep. Greg Landsman (D) is slightly favored to win his race, and Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D), a long-time target of Republicans, is in a “toss up” of her own.

Ohio Republicans are also contending with a scandal surrounding Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), who is facing allegations of domestic abuse. Miller denies the charges, but the controversy has put a once reliable red seat in play.

Republicans also fell short of their pick-up goals in Missouri, where a Republican-drawn map designed to flip the seat held by Democratic Rep. Emmanuel Cleaver was shot down by the courts.

Kondik said the cumulative effect of redistricting favors Republicans. But given the environment, they won’t realize anything close to the double-digit gains they envisioned when they launched their map- drawing campaign last year.

“As of now, we only have the Republicans netting 2-5 seats as a direct result of redistricting,” he said, “and if things are really bad in November, it may be even less than that.”

articles.title: MAP IT: DOJ illegal voting crackdown sweeps 17 states as razor-thin elections face scrutiny
articles.summary: The Justice Department charged 64 foreign nationals across 17 states with noncitizen voting and voter registration fraud in roughly five weeks.
articles.body: The Justice Department has charged 64 foreign nationals across 17 states with unlawful voting, fraudulent voter registration and election-related offenses in roughly the last five weeks, according to figures provided to Fox News Digital, as federal prosecutors intensify election-integrity enforcement. Minnesota leads the nation with 11 defendants, followed by Pennsylvania with 10 and Texas with nine. Louisiana accounts for five, while New Jersey, California and Florida each have four, according to the department's latest tally. The nationwide crackdown comes as federal officials intensify scrutiny of voter-registration safeguards ahead of November's midterms, with recent elections underscoring how even a few illegal ballots can exceed the margin separating candidates. Fox News Digital mapped the states with the largest concentrations of defendants as DOJ says it has charged 104 people with voting fraud-related offenses since Trump returned to office in 2025. SKID ROW FORGERIES, ILLEGAL VOTES AND A MAYORAL CANDIDATE: ELECTION FRAUD CASES PILE UP NATIONWIDE "Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen. In 2020, Iowa's 2nd Congressional District race was decided by six votes," a DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital, referring to Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' narrow victory over Democrat Rita Hart. DOJ said federal prosecutors are bringing more than twice as many election-fraud cases each week as the six-vote margin in the Iowa race. NIGERIAN WOMAN IN MASSACHUSETTS CHARGED AFTER ALLEGED ILLEGAL VOTING IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS The spokesperson added: "Voting by noncitizens and other ineligible voters is a federal crime, and the department will enforce the law whether a case involves one illegal ballot or hundreds." The cases involve allegations ranging from fraudulent registration applications to ballots cast in multiple elections. The department is also securing guilty pleas in some cases, including against Filipino national Evelyn Miller of Emmaus, Pennsylvania. Miller pleaded guilty to illegally voting in the 2024 presidential election and faces up to one year in prison and a $100,000 fine. MORE THAN A QUARTER-MILLION NONCITIZENS MAY BE REGISTERED TO VOTE IN 4 KEY STATES, DHS ALLEGES "We intend to prosecute anyone who corrupts our democracy by illegally voting in its elections," U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania David Metcalf said. Also in Pennsylvania, federal prosecutors charged Haitian national Cliff Sanon with submitting a fraudulent voter registration application in Philadelphia County. Prosecutors allege he submitted eight registration applications and voted in the November 2022 election. BLANCHE ANNOUNCES CHARGES AGAINST 10 PERMANENT RESIDENTS ACCUSED OF MINNESOTA VOTER FRAUD In Minnesota, Ghanaian green card holder Joshua Kofi Edzie was charged with illegally voting in the state's August 2026 primary and falsely claiming U.S. citizenship in connection with voter registration. The prosecutions have also reached Republican-led states, including Texas, Louisiana and Florida, which account for 18 defendants combined in the DOJ figures provided to Fox News Digital. In Louisiana, the feds indicted an ex-mayoral candidate on a charge of voting by an alien. Bridget Johnson, who ran in 2024 to lead Cotton Valley, Louisiana, allegedly submitted a registration in the name of Jamaican national Michael Wedderburn and falsely swore he was a citizen. Wedderburn then allegedly voted illegally in 2024 for president and mayor. He was also recently indicted. In New Jersey, Republicans have pointed to several razor-thin elections amid a separate controversy involving approximately 6,600 people who indicated they were not citizens but were erroneously registered through the state's Motor Vehicle Commission. Fewer than 400 subsequently voted, according to Gov. Mikie Sherrill's administration. Former Englewood Cliffs Mayor Mario Kranjac recently highlighted municipal elections in Caldwell, Atlantic Highlands and Bogota decided by margins of four to six votes in 2023. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The state has not established that any of the affected voters changed an election outcome. Sherrill spokesman Sean Higgins previously said the governor "moved with transparency and accountability to remediate this error from 2023." Authorities have not established that any of the cases identified in DOJ's nationwide tally changed the outcome of an election.

articles.title: Flock executive defends crime-fighting cameras as ACLU attorney questions company's motives amid backlash
articles.summary: Flock Safety touts dramatically higher crime clearance rates in cities using its cameras, but the ACLU raises serious privacy and constitutional concerns.
articles.body: Flock Safety, which operates controversial Flock cameras now in 49 states, is touting crime clearance rates in cities that use the cameras compared to cities that don't — as a nationwide battle over the surveillance tool rages. "It's used for any kind of crime really," Phil Arnold, a public affairs manager for the company, told Fox News Digital. "It's very helpful for hit-and-run accidents, also stolen vehicles, property crimes, crimes against people as well." Arnold is a retired law enforcement officer who served his community in Shorewood, Illinois, for 40 years. He was the chief police executive in the town for 27 years. FORMER PENTAGON AI CHIEF WARNS FLOCK CAMERAS COULD CREATE 'CHINA-LIKE SURVEILLANCE STATE' IN THE US Arnold told Fox News Digital that for the last seven years of his career, his department used automatic license plate reader (ALPR) technology, which Flock Safety operates, to help solve crimes, describing the innovation as nothing short of revolutionary. "Let me give you an example. Before we had this technology, someone would say, 'Hey, I just got robbed, and it was a white Chevy Tahoe,'" Arnold explained. "We would then put out this information, a BOLO [be on the lookout] so to speak, and police officers would stop every white Chevy Tahoe trying to find the offender." Now, in a similar situation, Flock surveillance cameras narrow the searches to a specific geographic location where a reported crime has occurred, and then photographs of license plates matching the vehicle description can be used to identify possible suspect vehicles. "So it narrows down the search," Arnold said. "It doesn't inconvenience the people who are just getting stopped because of the car they're driving." LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE Flock provided Fox News Digital data from an internal report regarding crime solving rates in cities that use Flock cameras, compared to cities that don't. For example, in Tennessee, Nashville cleared only 7% of motor vehicle thefts in the first half of 2026, versus 40% in Flock-equipped Hendersonville, a smaller city about 16 miles away, according to the data. "Aggravated assault clearance followed the same pattern: 41% vs. 95%. Only 3% of vehicle break-ins were solved in Nashville, compared with 50% in Hendersonville. Those patterns, according to Flock, hold true in places all over the country. Where Hillsborough, North Carolina, which does not use Flock, cleared 0% of vehicle thefts in the time studied, nearby Burlington cleared 46% of the same cases. In Flock-less Ann Arbor, Michigan, solve rates were lower than in nearby Van Buren Township. FLOCK CEO, TECH RIVAL CALLED OUT TO TESTIFY BEFORE SENATORS OVER AI CAMERA PRIVACY CONCERNS Flock described Eugene, Oregon, as "the most telling case." "Flock cameras ran through October 2025, then were removed," the report says. "Motor-vehicle-theft clearance fell from 15% to 9%; burglary clearance dropped from 21% to 15%. "Nearby Medford, still running Flock, cleared 29% of vehicle thefts & 25% of burglaries over the same period." But not everyone is singing Flock's praises. Skeptical communities nationwide have petitioned their local governments to do away with the technology. Some argue that it is intrusive and unnecessary, while others say it's unconstitutional. On Thursday, a federal judge in Oklahoma ruled that a police deputy who used Flock to access a woman's driving history over the previous month, and then used the historical data to pull her over, violated her Fourth Amendment rights. She was in possession of 91 pounds of methamphetamine at the time of the stop. FORMER SECRET SERVICE CYBERCRIME EXPERT WEIGHS IN ON PRIVACY AFTER HACKERS BREACH STOLEN FLOCK CAMERA Chad Marlow is a senior policy counsel at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), where his focus is privacy and surveillance. He argued there's not necessarily causation between implementing Flock cameras and solving crimes. "It's a different city. It's a different size. What were the auto theft rates beforehand? What are the poverty rates in that city?" he asked. "What are the philosophies of the police department? Like, how many police are dedicated to trying to prevent or solve car thefts in one city versus the other?" Privacy is a major question surrounding Flock cameras, and many places are having a robust debate on the level of surveillance they want on their streets, and whether their data should be collected by a private company working in tandem with the police. "I think a common misconception is that when the car goes past the camera, and it captures the image of the back of the vehicle and the license plate, which is all it does, you can't see who's driving the car, you can't see who the passenger is. It just captures the back of the car and the license plate," Arnold explained. INNOCENT WOMAN SAYS POLICE USE OF FLOCK CAMERA LED TO 13 DAYS IN JAIL He added that the data is not accessed except when law enforcement is searching for a suspect, and that police officers need a Computer Aided Dispatch (CAD) report or a case report number to access any data. The data is retained for 30 days, according to Arnold. But cases of police officers using ALPR technology for purposes outside its law enforcement scope are piling up. A Washington Post analysis identified at least 50 cases of rogue officers abusing the tool, with many cases involving stalking of ex-lovers. Meanwhile, the constitutionality of the surveillance remains up for debate. "The Constitution establishes our right to privacy, and it establishes that people's personal effects and their private information cannot be accessed by the government without a warrant, without probable cause," Marlow said, noting that it's not just Flock Safety using ALPR technology, and that companies like Axon and Motorola sell the technology, too. "But it's very fair for Americans to look out and be like, 'You know what, If I'm not accused of doing anything wrong, I don't want the government tracking everywhere I go in my vehicle for days, weeks, months, or even years. I don't want that happening, and even if the Constitution says it's allowed, I don't want my laws saying it's allowed.'" Arnold told Fox News Digital that Flock is open to government regulation of the tools. "We want legislation passed," he said. "Our CEO, Garrett Langley called, gosh, probably a month-and-a-half ago, asking legislators to please ... put the laws in place that will regulate this. "We want it regulated. We don't want people misusing the system. We've seen this in the news." He added: "Nobody dislikes a bad officer more than a good officer." Marlow says the company is asking for regulation to save its business amid the backlash it has recently received. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Flock suddenly coming to the table now is because they have no choice," he said, noting that company only recently declared that it would drop the standard data retention period to 30 days. "Flock didn't do that because it suddenly got a conscience, [or] it's suddenly decided to be ethical. It did it because it needed a PR bump." The bottom line for Arnold is that the tool helps police officers, and that help is desperately needed. "It's so good for the manpower of a police department, you know? Most police departments across the country are a little shorthanded. Not everybody wants to be the police anymore. So it truly does help in those cases," Arnold said. "It is a tool that is a force multiplier for sure, and I've seen that firsthand being a chief of police using the technology."

articles.title: Hurricane victim’s husband recalls watching wife die when tree crashed through home
articles.summary: “I watched the love of my life for 10 years go into the back of a coroner’s van and head down that road.”
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Joey Williams, the husband of a woman who died in Florida as Hurricane Isaias battered Gulf Coast states , is remembering his wife as an “ultra-nice bada– person” whom everyone loved.

Jenn Biggs Williams, 57, worked in human resources. She and Joey were married for a decade. She is the first known fatality of Hurricane Isaias, which struck the Gulf Coast over the weekend.

A person in Birmingham, Alabama, also died in connection with the storm, the Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency director confirmed.

Williams said that as the storm moved through, the couple went outside to take pictures of the sky and some of the damage it had caused. When they went back inside, a tree fell through the roof and into the living room, trapping both of them beneath it.

“I was able to squeeze out. My wife didn’t make it,” Williams told NewsNation. “The tree just fell on her and it was … we like to think it was pretty instant, you know? I mean, just gone. Gone.”

Williams said he was able to crawl out and began calling for his wife.

“I couldn’t … there’s nothing, you know?” he said.

He got a neighbor to help as the storm continued to produce winds of up to 100 mph.

“I’m like, ‘My wife’s trapped under the tree. Please, please,'” he said. “And, I mean, there’s nothing we can do.”

They called emergency services, but Williams said responders told him their ability to help was limited as the storm intensified. By the time crews arrived and were able to cut up the tree and pull her out, it was too late. The coroner’s office was called to the scene.

“They let me say bye to her,” he said. “I watched the love of my life for 10 years go into the back of a coroner’s van and head down that road. That’s the hardest thing I ever swallowed in my life.”

“Everybody loved her, right? Even her co-workers,” he said. “She was the ultra-nice bada– person.”

“I just want to hear her voice,” he continued. “I’ve called her phone five times just to tell her … she was my world.”

Sources told The New York Times on Saturday that the DOJ is investigating ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News for pulling their coverage days after a federal judge halted President Trump’s ban…
articles.body:
The Justice Department (DOJ) is investigating five major TV networks for alleged antitrust violations after the outlets briefly pulled their pool coverage.

Sources told The New York Times on Saturday that the DOJ is investigating ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News for pulling their coverage days after a federal judge halted President Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from reporting at the White House. This separate case is ongoing.

The Hill has reached out to the DOJ for comment.

A DOJ spokesperson told CNN that the group boycott among business competitors could violate U.S. law.

“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” the spokesperson told the outlet. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”

Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said the probe appears to be “a pretext for seeking records from the networks” on how they conduct their coverage of regular White House events amid Trump’s ban.

“The decisions news organizations make about coverage are protected by the First Amendment, and summoning antitrust authority, on top of the retaliatory actions the White House has already taken to bar certain outlets, is another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists,” Brown said in a statement .

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who extended the latest temporary injunction on Trump’s ban, is weighing whether to issue a longer-lasting injunction. The initial pause on the ban expired on Thursday.

The administration has made the familiar argument to justify Trump’s restriction, citing national security concerns and the use of anonymous sourcing. But the media outlets have pointed to the president’s frequent remarks that it was due to cumulative negative coverage, saying this was evidence of viewpoint discrimination by the government, which the First Amendment prohibits.

The White House also initially argued that the ban was in response to concerns over professionalism and not adhering to preset standards.

“The President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information,'” the DOJ attorneys representing Trump wrote in a court filing earlier this month.

Though the ban was lifted, CNN and Politico have both been blocked from boarding Air Force One and traveling with the president since. The media outlets’ attorney argues that this is causing harm to the two companies and must be addressed.

articles.title: El think tank liberal Institut Ostrom advierte sobre las promesas de Vox: "Hemos hecho las cuentas y es tramposo"
articles.standfirst: El organismo ha compartido un mensaje en su cuenta oficial de X
articles.summary: El organismo ha compartido un mensaje en su cuenta oficial de X
articles.body: El think tank liberal catalán Institut Ostrom ha advertido públicamente sobre la inviabilidad financiera de las propuestas económicas del partido político Vox. Según un análisis detallado publicado por la entidad en su sunat oficial de X, los recortes de gastos planteados por la formación son totalmente insuficientes para compensar la masiva reducción de impuestos que prometen. “Vox promete bajar el IRPF, el IVA y Sociedades, y dice que lo pagará recortando subvenciones y «paguitas». Hemos hecho las cuentas. La rebaja costaría unos 118.000 M€ al año: IRPF (exento hasta 22.000 €, luego 15% y 25%), unos 85.000 M€, con datos de la AEAT, IVA al 18% y al 8%, unos 16.000 M€ y Sociedades al 15 %, hasta 17.000 M€”, detalla, subrayado que el partidos liderado por Santiago Abascal sitúa el coste de su rebaja fiscal en una horquilla menor, de entre 64.000 y 70.000 millones de euros. “Ahora, los recortes. Suprimiendo por completo el IMV, la cooperación al desarrollo, las políticas activas de empleo, las becas y las ayudas a partidos, sindicatos y patronal, se ahorrarían 15.227 M€. Es apenas un 13% del coste”, prosigue. Finalmente, el organismo deja claro que, según su análisis, las matemáticas no salen: “Faltarían más de 100.000 M€. Sin más deuda, es tanto como la mitad del gasto en pensiones o toda la sanidad pública. Ni cerrando la educación pública entera se llegaría. Bajar impuestos puede ser buena política. Pero prometer que lo pagarán las subvenciones es tramposo”, sentencia. De esta manera, para financiar los más de 100.000 millones de euros restantes sin recurrir al endeudamiento, el Estado se vería obligado a recortar el equivalente a la mitad del gasto en pensiones, a la totalidad de la sanidad pública o a una cifra superior a todo el coste de la educación pública.

articles.title: Trump is waging all-out war against journalists
articles.summary: Shortly before returning to office after the 2024 race, Trump proclaimed, “LAWFARE IS DEAD.” But these days, lawfare is flourishing as never before.
articles.body:
Two weeks ago, Florida sued The New York Times , claiming that inadequate oversight jeopardized the paper’s reputation and hurt the value of state pension holders’ shares in the company.

Florida attorney general James Uthmeier (R) focused on what he called the paper’s “ incorrect and biased pro-Hamas coverage ” of the war in Gaza. The Times responded that although the suit is “positioned as a corporate governance petition to inspect the company’s books and records,” it was a “transparent attempt” to “chill journalism protected by the First Amendment.”

Winning the lawsuit may not be the point. The process alone damages the Times’s reputation and forces it to waste time, energy and money defending itself. And just the prospect of becoming the next target may encourage others to fall in line.

Ironically, Trump and his allies spent years alleging that his left-wing critics were weaponizing the law to damage his political prospects and hamper conservative causes. Trump insisted he was “ shocked ” by what he called Democrats’ “lawfare,” calling it “dirty,” “vicious” and a “third world” tactic.

Shortly before returning to office after the 2024 race, Trump proclaimed, “ LAWFARE IS DEAD .” But these days, lawfare is flourishing as never before.

Trump and his red-state allies have built an extraordinary web of coercive legal and regulatory initiatives directed at news organizations. Their arsenal includes lawsuits, subpoenas, search warrants, funding threats, license reviews, access restrictions, and regulatory agency investigations. Administration officials openly acknowledge that the goal is to “reshap[e] the media landscape” by achieving “Full Spectrum Dominance.”

The damage to a free press, an essential pillar of our democracy, is already substantial.

Trump called the media “ the enemy of the American people ” during his first term. Since returning to the White House, he has filed a $15 billion lawsuit against The New York Times and Penguin Random House for “industrial-scale defamation”; a $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal for reporting on a lewd birthday greeting he reportedly sent Jeffrey Epstein; and a $10 billion lawsuit against BBC over a documentary about the 2024 campaign.

According to an analysis by Axios , Trump, his administration and his businesses were involved in 16 media and defamation lawsuits last year and another nine so far in 2026. Many of Trump’s past lawsuits against the media have been dismissed on First Amendment grounds, and in one case Trump was ordered to pay The New York Times almost $400,000 in legal fees.

But Trump’s personal lawsuits are just the tip of the iceberg. Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House for reporting “ FICTION and LIES ,” after previously denying access to The Associated Press for refusing to accept his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico. The Defense Department has likewise restricted media access at the Pentagon and declared its press office off limits.

The day after Trump demanded that ABC fire comedian and Trump critic Jimmy Kimmel, the Federal Communications Commission ordered an accelerated review of all ABC station licenses, which otherwise would not have come up for renewal until 2028 or later. The commission, which has never before ordered such a sweeping review, insists it relates to ABC’s diversity and inclusion practices. ABC promptly sued the FCC , calling the review “blatant retaliation” for “the stories its journalists report and the viewpoints its network programs air.”

The FCC has also investigated the major broadcast networks for “news distortion” and what the agency considers potentially illegal diversity, equity and inclusion policies.

The Federal Trade Commission has launched its own investigations into allegations of online misinformation, driving up costs, hurting businesses and leading some entities to self-censor.

The Justice Department has subpoenaed the phone records of some journalists (and their relatives). And as part of an investigation into a government contractor suspected of mishandling classified information, FBI agents searched a Washington Post reporter’s home and seized her phone, laptops and other devices, even though she was not a target of the investigation.

Although courts have rejected many of these tactics, the campaign continues to accelerate, and red-state governments are joining in. In 2023, the attorneys general of Texas and Florida opened investigations into the liberal press watchdog Media Matters, apparently at the urging of Trump adviser Stephen Miller. And Florida’s shareholder rights suit against The New York Times has turned stock ownership into a vehicle for investigating editorial practices.

The right’s campaign against the press isn’t conventional lawfare. It doesn’t depend on winning in court. The parent companies of ABC and CBS paid millions to settle highly questionable lawsuits — one for defamation and the other over “deceitful editing” — probably because they were seeking required government approvals of major corporate transactions.

Trump’s message to the media is straightforward: Critical coverage now carries costs that go well beyond attorneys’ fees.

Trump was right about lawfare. It can be a “dirty” tactic when used to punish political adversaries. But when the plaintiff controls the entire machinery of government, including the Justice Department, the Pentagon, the FCC, the FTC and access to the White House, lawfare becomes far more dangerous: an existential threat to the institutions we depend on to hold the government accountable.

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.

articles.title: ‘Big Balls’ of DOGE fame gives exclusive look at new Trump mission to overhaul government
articles.summary: Edward Coristine reveals plans to make passport applications fully digital through America.gov, the AI-powered platform replacing thousands of sites.
articles.body: Edward Coristine, the former DOGE engineer better known as "Big Balls," is now helping build the Trump administration’s new digital front door to the federal government — an effort aimed at giving Americans one place to navigate information and, eventually, complete services now spread across thousands of government websites. "I think that the fact that there’s 29,000 government websites is pretty insane," Coristine told Fox News Digital in a sit-down interview. "And it is the citizens’ objective to have to go figure out which government website they’re supposed to use for each specific thing." Coristine — better known around Washington by his attention-grabbing "Big Balls" nickname — sat down with Fox News Digital at the White House to talk about his new role helping build America.gov, what he learned during his time at DOGE, the administration’s plans to make more government services fully digital, his experience being attacked in Washington, and how the nickname that helped make him famous actually came from his dad. TRUMP UNVEILS AMERICA.GOV AS AI-POWERED HUB FOR PASSPORTS, MEDICARE ENROLLMENT AND MORE Coristine is now working with the National Design Studio on the administration’s revamped America.gov, which launched Sept. 29 as an AI-powered single point of entry for information drawn from thousands of government websites. President Donald Trump singled out Coristine during the launch, identifying him as the project’s lead engineer and thanking him for his work. Coristine said his time at DOGE gave him a firsthand look at the frustration Americans face when trying to navigate federal services and helped shape what he is working on now. "I think we got a lot of feedback that the American government is hard to interact with because you have to navigate the maze of bureaucratic services," Coristine said. The software engineer had already worked in Musk’s orbit before joining DOGE, spending several months at Neuralink, Musk’s brain-computer interface company, before later joining the government efficiency effort at 19. "What I think is really special about America.gov is it presents a single point of entry to find all the information that you need," he added, including finding government services tailored to the user and asking questions with answers sourced from the federal government. TRUMP TO USHER IN ‘GOLDEN AGE’ OF AMERICAN TECH WITH DC BASH SHOWCASING POWERFUL NEW TOOL Coristine pointed to Medicare as one example, saying Americans currently may have to move between Medicare.gov and the Social Security website to enroll in benefits. "Companies, generally speaking, only have one website and everything is easy to find," he said. "We should have the same vision for the government." The ambitions for America.gov also go beyond simply helping users find the right information. Coristine said the administration plans to make first-time passport applications fully digital, expanding beyond the online renewal system already available to eligible Americans. "Specifically with passports, what we’re going to do is we’re gonna make new passports online for the first time ever," Coristine said, describing the existing process as "very manual." TRUMP’S NEW HIGH-TECH GOVERNMENT HUB HOLDS SOME BIZARRE SURPRISES: ‘ENJOY FINDING THEM’ "You have to go in person, you have to get to the post office, you get your photo taken like a CVS or Walgreens," he said. Under the planned system, Coristine said users would be able to take their passport photo at home, preview how it would appear on the document and complete the process "without leaving the America.gov website." Coristine also offered a glimpse into how Trump has talked about the broader project, comparing the president’s approach to digital government with his background in hospitality. "I think the president has been a great host for his entire career. He’s been in the hospitality business, right?" Coristine said. "So any great host knows they have to make things easy, they have to make it all feel clean." ELON MUSK LANDS NEW TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ROLE SHAPING FUTURE OF AMERICAN WARFARE "President Trump is very focused on removing the potholes from the digital government that make it hard to get things done," he added. The role marks the latest chapter in a whirlwind stint in Washington that began at DOGE and quickly thrust the 20-year-old — and his now-famous "Big Balls" nickname — into the national spotlight. Coristine told Fox News Digital the "Big Balls" moniker had a far less dramatic origin than its eventual notoriety might suggest. "I got the nickname Big Balls from my dad," he said, explaining that he eventually made it his LinkedIn URL AND THIS IS WHAT DROVE IT INTO THE NATIONAL SPOTLIGHT, RIGHT? "It was actually, like, fairly underground, but I was discovered," Coristine said. "It’s been very funny ever since." EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE THE SECRETIVE MINE DOGE HELPED DRAG OUT OF A DECADES-OLD BUREAUCRATIC BLACK HOLE Coristine’s profile rose further in August 2025 after he was attacked while walking a female friend back to her car in Washington’s Logan Circle neighborhood, an incident that left him with a broken nose and concussion and drew national attention. Coristine has said he rushed his friend into the car before the group turned on him, slamming him against the vehicle and throwing punches. "I really thank President Trump for making D.C. safe again," Coristine said. "Like all my friends, they’re now able to walk outside." "Everyone is very calmed by the National Guard because it feels like the city is so much safer," he continued. "And the crime numbers totally represent that. The crime has been falling like a knife in D.C." Trump established the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force in March 2025 before launching an intensified federal crime crackdown in August, with the operation delivering more than 16,000 arrests, 3,200 narcotics arrests and nearly 2,000 illegal firearms seized in its first year. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "So I’m unbelievably grateful to the president for making the city safe and beautiful," Coristine said.

articles.title: Trump names Katie Bailey as White House legislative affairs director
articles.summary: President Trump on Saturday named Katie Bailey as the White House’s legislative affairs director, months after former director James Braid vacated the role ahead of the November midterm elections. Trump wrote on Truth Social that Bailey, as deputy director, “has already delivered strong results” in assisting with the confirmations of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin,…
articles.body:
President Trump on Saturday named Katie Bailey as the White House’s legislative affairs director, months after former director James Braid vacated the role ahead of the November midterm elections.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that Bailey, as deputy director, “has already delivered strong results” in assisting with the confirmations of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling .

“After previously working on Capitol Hill, Katie understands how the Executive and Legislative Branches of Government can most effectively work together to achieve Great Success for the American People,” Trump wrote. “Katie will take the place of James Braid, my longest tenured Legislative Affairs Director, who has done a fabulous job, and is now going into the private sector, where he will be very successful.”

“I know Katie will be fantastic, and work tirelessly with Congress to pass Bills that help, MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN, GREATER THAN EVER BEFORE,” the president’s post concludes. “Good luck Katie!”

The announcement comes after Trump announced conservative commentator Katie Zacharia was named as the new White House press secretary.

Braid congratulated Bailey on the social platform X , noting her past work with other Republican lawmakers, including Sen. Mike Braun (R-Ind.).

“Katie’s a consummate pro, an extraordinary hill operator, and one of the best people in Washington,” Braid wrote. “Katie is going to do great things, and I know that the Office of Legislative Affairs will deliver for the President under her leadership.”

Braid played a key role in ushering major pieces of Trump’s legislative agenda through Congress, including the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, as well as Trump’s judicial nominees. Braid was also a key link between Trump’s and Vice President Vance’s orbits going into the president’s second administration.

Vance praised Braid when announcing his departure, saying that he has “been with me in every fight I’ve been in, from day one in my Senate office through the transition and the president’s transformative second term.”

“He has served the President with distinction and I couldn’t be prouder of him,” Vance said in a post on X.

Bailey enters the role as Republicans face an uphill battle to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s partner, projects a 76 percent probability that Democrats win back the House, while they have a 56 percent probability of reclaiming the Senate.

articles.title: Emmer says he’s ‘so happy’ Trump will decide whether to stream public execution
articles.summary: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) on Sunday said he is “so happy” that President Trump will decide on whether to livestream the execution by firing squad of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan. “I am so happy that we have a president, a chief executive in this country, who will make a decision which…
articles.body:
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) on Sunday said he is “so happy” that President Trump will decide on whether to livestream the execution by firing squad of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan.

“I am so happy that we have a president, a chief executive in this country, who will make a decision which is in the best interest of the American people,” Emmer, who prefaced by saying he does not favor the death penalty, told ABC News’s Jonathan Karl on “This Week.”

“He will hold the criminals and the terrorists accountable,” Emmer continued. “And, frankly, if you come to this country or you’re radicalized in this country to kill Americans and disrupt our way of life, there should be significant consequences.”

Trump had said Saturday that he will “ make a decision ultimately ” about livestreaming the execution.

“There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it, because you know by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

Last week, a White House spokesperson confirmed that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “recommended” Hasan’s execution be carried out by firing squad on Dec. 3, and the president “approved” it.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center in November 2009, killing 12 soldiers and one civilian. He injured 32 others in what was the deadliest mass shooting ever on a U.S. military installation.

Hasan acted as his own attorney during his 2013 trial, saying in his opening statement that the “evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter,” adding that he carried out the mass shooting in response to the U.S. wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

The last execution by firing squad in the U.S. was of Army Pvt. Eddie Slovik in 1945. He was convicted of desertion — one of the 40,000 service members to desert during World War II, the Los Angeles Review of Books wrote in a 2014 retrospective of the film “The Execution of Private Slovik,” starring Martin Sheen. Slovik’s execution was the first for a soldier convicted of desertion since the Civil War.

Since then, the last U.S. military execution was of Army Pvt. John A. Bennett in 1961. Bennett was hanged after being convicted of rape and attempted murder, according to the Death Penalty Information Center , a national nonprofit organization focused on the death penalty.

Vice President Vance told reporters Friday that he will not be watching the execution if it is approved to be livestreamed. He added that he did not “know that that’s actually going to happen.”

articles.title: Mullin says livestreaming Hasan execution is part of ‘restoring American values’
articles.summary: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin stood behind the Trump administration’s decision to livestream the military execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, despite growing bipartisan criticism over the plan. In an interview with CBS News’s “Face the Nation” on Sunday, Mullin dismissed concerns coming from across party lines that publicizing Hasan’s…
articles.body:
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin stood behind the Trump administration’s decision to livestream the military execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, despite growing bipartisan criticism over the plan.

In an interview with CBS News’s “Face the Nation” on Sunday, Mullin dismissed concerns coming from across party lines that publicizing Hasan’s death by firing squad could inspire extremists or turn the convicted mass murderer into a martyr.

“First of all, no one has to watch it,” Mullin said when asked whether livestreaming the execution in Texas could pose a threat to national security.

Pressed on why Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth would move to broadcast the execution, Mullin pointed to President Trump’s leadership.

“I follow President Trump. He’s a commander in chief of the country, and he does a phenomenal job,” Mullin said. “He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he’s restoring American values.”

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) urged the Pentagon chief Friday to reverse the decision, warning that livestreaming the execution could bolster his notoriety and fulfill his wish for martyrdom.

“There is no need to livestream any execution, including this one,” Murkowski wrote on social media Friday. “I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America.”

CBS News host Margaret Brennan pressed Mullin on Murkowski’s warning, as well as concern from Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer (N.D) who said the livestream could potentially fuel radicalization.

The DHS leader replied by saying he did not believe the move posed an increased security threat.

“I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” he said. “I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime.”

“I have no sympathy for him, and I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies,” Mullin added.

Trump told reporters Saturday that he will “ make a decision ultimately ” on whether to go through with the livestream and has said he “absolutely” approves of the execution.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood in Texas. He was convicted in 2013 of 45 counts of premeditated and attempted murder and sentenced to death.

His execution, scheduled for Dec. 3, will mark the first military execution in more than six decades.

articles.title: Hamilton says Vance’s attacks on his religion are ‘really sad,’ ‘pathetic’
articles.summary: Kansas Senate candidate Adam Hamilton (D) on Sunday clapped back at Vice President Vance’s attacks on his religious beliefs, calling the attacks “really sad” and “pathetic.” ABC’s Jonathan Karl sat down to interview Hamilton in the Sunflower State and asked the moderate pastor about Vance, who has been outspoken about his religious beliefs since before…
articles.body:
Kansas Senate candidate Adam Hamilton (D) on Sunday clapped back at Vice President Vance’s attacks on his religious beliefs, calling the attacks “really sad” and “pathetic.”

ABC’s Jonathan Karl sat down to interview Hamilton in the Sunflower State and asked the moderate pastor about Vance, who has been outspoken about his religious beliefs since before entering politics, coming to campaign for Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.).

“He really went after you,” Karl said. “He called your views ‘left-wing radicalism dressed in the skin suit of our religion.’ Saying that of your beliefs: ‘That is not Christianity.’ This was the vice president of the United States taking aim at your religious practice.”

“Well, I thought it was a sign of desperation and I thought it was really sad,” Hamilton replied. “It was pathetic. He doesn’t know me, doesn’t know anything about my faith. He came in attacking –– when do we start attacking people’s faith?”

Hamilton brushed the criticism aside, saying that he wakes up every day, “I slip to my knees, I offer my life to Christ, I pray for the Holy Spirit to lead me, I read scripture, I carry the Bible with me everywhere I go.” He pulled a small Bible from his back pocket during the interview.

“I not only seek to be a follower of Jesus, but to practice that in how I treat other people,” Hamilton said. “And I just would say examine my life, examine the way I’ve tried to live and then I want to see, Mr. Vice President, let’s compare. Let’s compare theology. Let’s compare our faith and the impact we’re having on the world.”

The Kansas Democrat added that Vance’s additional criticisms accusing Hamilton of suggesting that “it’s a sin to be white and a sin to raise cattle and eat feet” and that he believes it’s “OK with supporting groups that spit on God-fearing Americans” were not true.

“Yeah, so every single line of what you just read was a lie,” Hamilton said in response. “It was a false hit. It was, like, 180 degrees different from reality. So there was no part of what he said was true.”

During the rally for Marshall in Olathe, Kan., last Monday, Vance played soundbites of past sermons Hamilton gave that lacked context, indicating that the pastor thinks people should repent from eating meat, while also slamming Hamilton’s church for holding a local pride festival, the Kansas Reflector reported .

“In this race, we have got Dr. Roger Marshall, a proud servant of this state, and a proud Christian to boot, versus a guy who would insult your faith and spit on your religion to accrue donations to himself,” Vance said.

Hamilton’s campaign has invited Vance to come to his church “instead of attacking the largest United Methodist Church in the country,” spokesperson Glynnis Harvey told the Reflector.

If elected, Hamilton would be the first Democrat elected by Kansans to the Senate since former Sen. George McGill (D-Kan.) in 1932.
